etymology: From Old English wid, broad, extensive. Webster 1828: broad; having a great extent each way; remote; distant. Our Lord uses it once, of a gate, and set it against strait in the most quoted contrast in the Sermon on the Mount.
biblical_def: Wide is fixed in Christian memory by a single verse: Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat (Matthew 7:13). The following verse gives the alternative and its arithmetic: strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it (Matthew 7:14). Four contrasts, exactly parallel — wide against strait, broad against narrow, destruction against life, many against few. The wide gate is not described as attractive; it is described as easy and as crowded, and the two things are related. Scripture uses the word elsewhere in a happier sense. God says to a people He has just reminded of the Exodus, open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it (Psalm 81:10) — an invitation to ask largely of a God who gives largely. Proverbs uses it drily of domestic misery: better a corner of the housetop than with a brawling woman in a wide house (Proverbs 21:9). Room is no comfort where peace is absent, which is the same lesson the wide gate teaches on a larger scale.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WIDE as broad; having a great extent each way; and, as an adverb, at a distance, far from the mark, as to shoot wide. Both the spatial and the figurative senses of straying from the mark are useful in reading Matthew 7:13.
webster_full: WIDE, a. — Broad; having a great extent each way; as a wide plain, a wide field.
Remote; distant; far apart; as, the two opinions are wide of each other.
WIDE, adv. — At a distance; far from the mark or purpose; as, to shoot wide of the target.
The adverbial sense of missing the mark is close to the biblical idea of sin as a falling short, though the words are unrelated.
The Authorized Version’s strait in Matthew 7:13 means narrow or confined, not straight; the two are different words and the confusion is very old.
scriptures: Matthew 7:13
Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat:
Matthew 7:14
Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.
Psalm 81:10
I am the LORD thy God, which brought thee out of the land of Egypt: open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it.
Proverbs 21:9
It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.
Jeremiah 6:8
Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee; lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited.
corruption_summary: Matthew 7:13-14 states plainly that the saved are few and the lost many, and it is one of the least preached texts in the modern pulpit — avoided by universalists who deny it and by growth-minded churches whose whole method assumes the opposite.
corruption_paragraphs: Many there be which go in thereat, and few there be that find it. Our Lord says it in the same sermon in which He gives the Beatitudes, and He says it immediately before warning about false prophets in sheep’s clothing and about men who will plead their ministries at the judgment. Universalism cannot accommodate the verse and simply sets it aside. But a subtler evasion is more common among the orthodox: the assumption that numerical breadth is itself a mark of divine blessing, so that the crowded road is read as evidence of success. Christ attaches the crowd to the wide gate, not to the narrow one. This is not an argument for celebrating small congregations, still less for the sourness that mistakes obscurity for faithfulness; it is a warning that popularity is not evidence either way, and that the only test is the gate.

The strait gate must not be misheard as a gate of difficulty to be earned. Christ says elsewhere I am the door, and the narrowness of the gate is the narrowness of one Person and one way, not the narrowness of a rigorous entrance fee. What cannot be carried through it is baggage — self-righteousness, other saviours, the reservation of a beloved sin. Bunyan understood the passage exactly when he sent his pilgrim to a wicket gate with a burden that had to fall off before the Cross. And the same God who narrows the gate says open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it; He is strict about the door and lavish inside it.
roots_summary: Greek platus (G4116), broad, and euruchoros (G2149), spacious, in Matthew 7:13; Hebrew rachab (H7342), broad, wide, roomy.
roots_lines: Greek platus (G4116) — broad; whence plateia, a broad way or street.
Greek euruchoros (G2149) — spacious, wide in room; the word rendered broad at Matthew 7:13.
Greek stenos (G4728) — narrow, strait; the gate of Matthew 7:13-14 and Luke 13:24.
Greek tethlimmene — compressed, hemmed in; the participle behind narrow is the way, from the verb for tribulation.
Hebrew rachab (H7342) — broad, wide; open thy mouth wide (Psalm 81:10).
usage: Wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction (Matthew 7:13) — ease and crowds together.
Few there be that find it (Matthew 7:14) — the arithmetic our Lord attached to the two roads.
Open thy mouth wide, and I will fill it (Psalm 81:10) — the same word turned to invitation.

etymology: From Old English slaw, sluggish, dull. Webster 1828: moving a small distance in a long time; not ready; not prompt; dull; inactive. In Scripture it is one of the great words of the divine character — slow to anger — and one of the sharpest words of rebuke — slow of heart to believe.
biblical_def: Slow is used of God with reverence and of men with reproach. When the LORD proclaimed His name to Moses in the cleft of the rock, the second attribute after mercy was longsuffering, and the phrase that carries it through the Old Testament is slow to anger: The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy (Psalm 103:8). Nehemiah’s great prayer of confession says the same of a God dealing with a people who had appointed a captain to return to Egypt: thou art a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not (Nehemiah 9:17). God’s slowness here is not weakness or indifference; it is deliberate forbearance while judgment is deserved, and Peter says the same thing of the delay of the second advent — the Lord is not slack concerning his promise… but is longsuffering to us-ward. James then commands the imitation of it in the most practical terms in the epistle: let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19). And the risen Christ uses the word as a rebuke on the Emmaus road: O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken (Luke 24:25).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SLOW as moving a small distance in a long time; not swift; not ready; not prompt or quick; dull; inactive; tardy. He also gives the sense of being late or behindhand, which is exactly what 2 Peter 3:9 denies of God.
webster_full: SLOW, a. — Moving a small distance in a long time; not swift; not quick in motion.
Not ready; not prompt or quick; as slow of speech, slow to anger.
Dull; inactive; tardy; late; behind in time.
Not hasty; acting with deliberation; a sense in which slowness is a virtue and not a defect.
The last sense is the biblical one when the word is used of God: deliberate forbearance, not tardiness.
scriptures: Psalm 103:8
The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy.
Nehemiah 9:17

And refused to obey, neither were mindful of thy wonders that thou didst among them; but hardened their necks, and in their rebellion appointed a captain to return to their bondage: but thou art a God ready to pardon, gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and forsookest them not.
James 1:19
Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath:
Luke 24:25
Then he said unto them, O fools, and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken:
Exodus 34:6
And the LORD passed by before him, and proclaimed, The LORD, The LORD God, merciful and gracious, longsuffering, and abundant in goodness and truth,
corruption_summary: God’s slowness to anger is regularly heard as mildness — a God who does not really get angry — when Scripture means a God whose anger is real, deserved, and deliberately delayed.
corruption_paragraphs: The Hebrew behind slow to anger is literally long of nostrils, a figure for a long fuse; the anger is presumed and its arrival is postponed. Exodus 34, the very proclamation of mercy and grace and longsuffering, ends by saying that He will by no means clear the guilty. Both clauses are the same self-revelation. A God who is slow to anger is not a God incapable of it, and a mercy that has no wrath behind it is not mercy but indifference. This matters because the modern instinct is to purchase divine kindness by denying divine judgment, and the trade always fails: a God who cannot be provoked cannot be reconciled either, and the cross becomes unintelligible.

James turns the attribute into a command and puts it where it does the most work. Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath is written to a scattered church with real grievances, and the order is deliberate: listening first, speech delayed, anger delayed longest. He adds the reason, for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God, which forecloses the standard defence that one is angry on God’s behalf. And Luke 24:25 supplies the one slowness Christ rebukes. Slow to speak is a virtue; slow of heart to believe what the prophets have spoken is folly, and He cured it not by comfort but by expounding in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself.
roots_summary: Hebrew erek appayim, long of nostrils, that is slow to anger; Greek bradus (G1021), slow, in James 1:19 and Luke 24:25.
roots_lines: Hebrew erek (H750) — long, patient; joined to aph, the nostril, for the idiom slow to anger.
Hebrew aph (H639) — the nose or nostril, and by extension anger, from the flaring of the nostrils.
Greek bradus (G1021) — slow, dull; slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19).
Greek braduno (G1019) — to be slow, to delay; the Lord is not slack concerning his promise (2 Peter 3:9) uses the related bradun.
Greek makrothumia (G3115) — longsuffering, long-tempered; the New Testament equivalent of the Hebrew idiom.
usage: Slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy (Psalm 103:8) — deliberate forbearance, not mildness.
Swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath (James 1:19) — the attribute turned into a command.
O fools, and slow of heart to believe (Luke 24:25) — the one slowness Christ rebukes.

etymology: From Old English sarig, feeling pain, from sar, sore; unrelated to sorrow despite the modern association. Webster 1828: grieved for the loss of some good; pained for some evil; also, poor, mean, vile, as a sorry excuse. The Authorized Version uses the first sense, and Paul builds a whole doctrine of repentance on it.
biblical_def: Sorry in the Authorized Version means grieved, and 2 Corinthians 7 is the passage that gives it doctrinal weight. Paul had written a severe letter, and he reflects on it with unusual candour: though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season (2 Corinthians 7:8). He then distinguishes what happened next: I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner (7:9), and states the principle that has governed Reformed pastoral practice ever since — godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death (7:10). Two sorrows, one leading to life and one to death, distinguished not by intensity but by direction. Herod supplies the counter-example in a single line: hearing the request for John’s head, the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her (Matthew 14:9). Real grief, no repentance, murder committed anyway. And Nehemiah forbids the wrong sorrow on a day of covenant renewal: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SORRY as grieved for the loss of some good, or pained for some evil; and, in a second sense, poor, mean, vile, worthless — as a sorry fellow. Only the first sense appears in the Authorized Version.
webster_full: SORRY, a. — Grieved for the loss of some good; pained for some evil that has happened.
Melancholy; dismal; as, a sorry sight.
Poor; mean; vile; worthless; as, a sorry excuse, a sorry fellow.
Webster notes the word is from the Saxon sarig, from sar, sore, and is not from sorrow, with which it is commonly confounded.
The modern conversational use of sorry as an apology is a late development and is not the biblical sense at all.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 7:8
For though I made you sorry with a letter, I do not repent, though I did repent: for I perceive that the same epistle hath made you sorry, though it were but for a season.
2 Corinthians 7:9
Now I rejoice, not that ye were made sorry, but that ye sorrowed to repentance: for ye were made sorry after a godly manner, that ye might receive damage by us in nothing.
2 Corinthians 7:10
For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death.
Matthew 14:9
And the king was sorry: nevertheless for the oath’s sake, and them which sat with him at meat, he commanded it to be given her.
Nehemiah 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
corruption_summary: The reduction of repentance to an apology is the defining pastoral corruption of the age, and 2 Corinthians 7:10 is the text that dismantles it: two sorrows, one working salvation and one working death.
corruption_paragraphs: The public apology has become a genre with recognizable conventions: regret expressed, harm acknowledged, feelings validated, and nothing whatever changed. Paul’s test is different. He lists what godly sorrow produced in Corinth — carefulness, clearing of themselves, indignation, fear, vehement desire, zeal, revenge — seven fruits, every one of them active. Worldly sorrow produces feeling and stops there, and Paul says it works death. The difference is not that one grief is deeper. Judas felt more than Peter did, went out, confessed openly that he had betrayed innocent blood, returned the money, and hanged himself. Esau sought the blessing carefully with tears and found no place of repentance. Sorrow that terminates on the sinner’s own distress has nowhere to go.

Herod is the shortest case study in Scripture. The king was sorry, and then he had John beheaded to save face in front of his guests. His grief was genuine, his conscience was working, and it moved nothing, because the pressure of the company at his table outweighed it. That is worldly sorrow in one verse, and it names the mechanism precisely: the fear of man. Paul’s converse comfort is that godly sorrow leads to a repentance not to be repented of — a turning no one ever regrets afterward. And Nehemiah shows the limit: on the day the law was read and the people wept, they were told not to be sorry, because the joy of the LORD was their strength. Conviction has a purpose and a terminus, and the terminus is joy.
roots_summary: Greek lupeo (G3076), to grieve or make sorrowful, and lupe (G3077), sorrow, in 2 Corinthians 7; the English word is from Old English sarig, sore.
roots_lines: Greek lupeo (G3076) — to grieve, to make sorry; used five times in 2 Corinthians 7:8-11.
Greek lupe (G3077) — sorrow, grief; godly sorrow and the sorrow of the world are the same noun with different qualifiers.
Greek metanoia (G3341) — repentance, a change of mind; what godly sorrow works.
Greek ametameletos (G278) — not to be repented of, not regretted; repentance to salvation not to be repented of.
Old English sarig, from sar, sore — the English word is unrelated to sorrow, which comes from sorg, care.
usage: Godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation (2 Corinthians 7:10) — the distinction the whole doctrine rests on.
The king was sorry: nevertheless… he commanded it (Matthew 14:9) — grief that changed nothing.
Neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength (Nehemiah 8:10) — conviction has a terminus.

etymology: From Latin finire, to end, from finis, an end or boundary. Webster 1828: ended; completed; perfected; polished to the highest degree. The word stands at three great terminals in Scripture — the finished creation, the finished work of Christ, and the finished course of a servant.
biblical_def: Finished marks completions, and Scripture places three of them where a reader cannot miss them. The first closes creation: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them (Genesis 2:1), and God rested, not from weariness but because the work was done. The second is the sixth word from the cross, and in the Greek it is a single word: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost (John 19:30). It is not a sigh of exhaustion but the merchant’s and the servant’s word for a debt discharged and a task completed. He had already said it to the Father in the upper room, in the past tense, before He went to Gethsemane: I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do (John 17:4). The third is Paul’s, from a Roman cell, with execution near: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). One finished work purchases salvation; the other finished course is the evidence of a life laid hold of by it, and the two must never be confused or the gospel is lost.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines FINISHED as ended, completed, perfected, and adds the sense of being polished to the highest degree of excellence — as a finished performance. Both senses are present in It is finished: the work ended, and nothing wanting in it.
webster_full: FINISHED, pp. — Ended; completed; done; perfected.
Polished to the highest degree of excellence; as a finished poem, a finished education.
FINISH, v.t. — To arrive at the end of, in performance; to complete; to bring to an end.
To perfect; to bestow the last touches on; to render complete and excellent.
The commercial force of the Greek behind John 19:30 — a debt marked paid in full — is not conveyed by any single English word, but Webster’s completed and perfected together come near it.
scriptures: Genesis 2:1
Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.
John 17:4
I have glorified thee on the earth: I have finished the work which thou gavest me to do.
John 19:30
When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
2 Timothy 4:7
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith:
Hebrews 10:14
For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
corruption_summary: Every religion of human merit is a denial that the work is finished, and so is every Protestant conscience that keeps re-opening a settled account — Rome’s continuing sacrifice on one side, and the believer’s habit of re-crucifying Christ in his own guilt on the other.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman mass is defined as a true and proper propitiatory sacrifice offered for the living and the dead, and the Reformers judged it a denial of John 19:30 for that reason. Hebrews argues at length that the levitical priests stood daily offering the same sacrifices which can never take away sins, but that this Man, after He had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down. Sitting is the posture the argument turns on; there was no seat in the tabernacle because the priest’s work was never done. By one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. Purgatory, indulgences, the treasury of merit, and the continuing sacrifice all rest on the assumption that something remains to be paid, and the single Greek word from the cross is the answer to all four.

The Protestant version of the same error is quieter and troubles more consciences. A believer who accepts justification by faith alone as a doctrine may still live as though today’s failure re-opened the account, and treat his assurance as rising and falling with his performance. The remedy is not to think less of the failure but to think more of the finishing. Christ said It is finished before He gave up the ghost, and He said I have finished the work before Gethsemane, and the resurrection was the Father’s receipt. Paul’s I have finished my course belongs to a different order entirely: it is the fruit of the first finishing, not a contribution to it.
roots_summary: Greek teleo (G5055), to bring to an end, to complete, to pay; the perfect tetelestai at John 19:30; Hebrew kalah (H3615), to be complete, at Genesis 2:1.
roots_lines: Greek teleo (G5055) — to finish, complete, accomplish, and in commercial use to pay in full.
Greek tetelestai — the perfect passive at John 19:30: it has been finished and stands finished.
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to perfect, to bring to the goal; I have finished the work (John 17:4).
Greek dromos (G1408) — a course, a race-track; I have finished my course (2 Timothy 4:7).
Hebrew kalah (H3615) — to be complete, to be at an end; the heavens and the earth were finished (Genesis 2:1).
usage: Thus the heavens and the earth were finished (Genesis 2:1) — the first completion, followed by rest.
It is finished (John 19:30) — one Greek word, a debt discharged.
I have finished my course (2 Timothy 4:7) — the servant’s completion, which is fruit and not payment.

etymology: From Old English warnian, to take heed, to give notice of danger. Webster 1828: to give notice of approaching or probable danger; to caution against evil. In Ezekiel it is the whole duty of a watchman, and in Paul it is an inseparable part of preaching Christ.
biblical_def: Warn is the watchman’s verb, and Ezekiel 3 states the office and its terms with a severity found nowhere else in Scripture. Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me (Ezekiel 3:17). Then the two cases. If the watchman does not warn the wicked, the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand (3:18). If he does warn and the man does not turn, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul (3:19). The watchman is not accountable for the response; he is wholly accountable for the warning. Paul takes the office into the New Testament without softening it. To the Ephesian elders he said, by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears (Acts 20:31) — and had already told them he was pure from the blood of all men, which is Ezekiel’s language exactly. And warning is not a supplement to gospel preaching but part of it: Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus (Colossians 1:28). To Corinth he adds the tone: I write not these things to shame you, but as my beloved sons I warn you.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WARN as to give notice of approaching or probable danger or evil, that it may be avoided; to caution against evil practices; and to admonish of a duty. All three senses are Ezekiel’s and Paul’s.
webster_full: WARN, v.t. — To give notice of approaching or probable danger or evil, that it may be avoided.
To caution against evil practices; to admonish; as, to warn a man against intemperance.
To admonish of a duty neglected; to give notice to appear, as in a legal summons.
To notify by authority; the older civic sense, as to warn a town meeting.
The legal senses are worth keeping in mind: a warning in Scripture is an official act performed under authority, not merely friendly advice.
scriptures: Ezekiel 3:17
Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.
Ezekiel 3:18

When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, nor speakest to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand.
Ezekiel 3:19
Yet if thou warn the wicked, and he turn not from his wickedness, nor from his wicked way, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul.
Colossians 1:28
Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom; that we may present every man perfect in Christ Jesus:
Acts 20:31
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
corruption_summary: Warning has been reclassified as unloving, and a great deal of contemporary preaching has quietly dropped it — which, on Ezekiel’s terms, transfers the blood from the hearer’s account to the preacher’s.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern objection is that warning is negative, judgmental, and drives people away, and that the winsome course is to accentuate the invitation. Ezekiel 3 forecloses the argument by making warning a matter of the watchman’s own life. The watchman who says nothing is not neutral; the wicked man dies either way, and in one case the watchman is charged with his blood. Notice also what the warning is for: to save his life. It is an act of love by definition, and the man on the wall who sees the army and stays silent to avoid alarming the city has not been kind. The tone is prescribed too — Paul warned night and day with tears, and wrote to Corinth not to shame you, but as my beloved sons. Severity without affection is not the model; neither is affection without severity.

Colossians 1:28 settles where warning belongs in the message. Whom we preach, warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom — the warning is part of preaching Christ, not an appendix bolted on for the hard-hearted. A gospel presented as an improvement to a life that was otherwise going well requires no warning, which is exactly why so much preaching has none. Where men are told what they actually are before God, the warning writes itself, and so does the sweetness of the remedy. The Puritans were the great practitioners of this, and the reason their warnings could be so searching is that their view of Christ was so large.
roots_summary: Hebrew zahar (H2094), to warn, to admonish, and also to shine or teach; Greek noutheteo (G3560), to put in mind, to admonish; tsaphah (H6822), to watch, gives watchman.
roots_lines: Hebrew zahar (H2094) — to admonish, to warn; the verb repeated through Ezekiel 3 and 33.
Hebrew tsaphah (H6822) — to look out, to keep watch; tsopheh is the watchman of Ezekiel 3:17.
Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to put in mind, to admonish, to warn; Colossians 1:28, Acts 20:31, 1 Thessalonians 5:14.
Greek nouthesia (G3559) — admonition; bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4).
Hebrew dam mi-yad — blood at the hand; the idiom of accountability in Ezekiel 3:18 and Acts 20:26.
usage: His blood will I require at thine hand (Ezekiel 3:18) — the cost of a warning withheld.
Thou hast delivered thy soul (Ezekiel 3:19) — the watchman is answerable for the warning, not the response.
Warning every man, and teaching every man in all wisdom (Colossians 1:28) — warning as part of preaching Christ.

etymology: From Old English withstandan, to stand against — with in its older sense of against, preserved also in withhold and withdraw. Webster 1828: to oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force. Paul uses it for the believer’s posture in the evil day and for his own rebuke of Peter at Antioch.
biblical_def: Withstand means to stand against, and the New Testament’s chief use is defensive: take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand (Ephesians 6:13). The whole armour passage never commands an advance; it commands standing, three times, and the armour is given because the enemy is not flesh and blood. The second use is a scene rather than a doctrine, and it has governed Protestant thinking about authority ever since: when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11). Peter had withdrawn from eating with the Gentiles for fear of them of the circumcision, and Paul says even Barnabas was carried away with the dissimulation. The rebuke was public, to the face, and Paul’s reason was that the truth of the gospel was at stake. The Old Testament supplies the warning against withstanding wrongly: Abijah told Jeroboam’s army, ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves (2 Chronicles 13:8). Numbers and calves against a covenant — the odds were the other way.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WITHSTAND as to oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force; and notes the composition of with in its sense of against with stand. The word means holding ground, not attacking.
webster_full: WITHSTAND, v.t. — To oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force.
The prefix with here carries its ancient sense of against, as it does in withhold, withdraw, and withsay.
The word denotes holding one’s ground against pressure rather than advancing upon an enemy.
Ephesians 6:13 pairs it with stand: to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Webster’s inclusion of moral force is important; Galatians 2:11 is a withstanding entirely of speech and truth.
scriptures: Ephesians 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Galatians 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
2 Chronicles 13:8
And now ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD in the hand of the sons of David; and ye be a great multitude, and there are with you golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods.
Daniel 11:15

So the king of the north shall come, and cast up a mount, and take the most fenced cities: and the arms of the south shall not withstand, neither his chosen people, neither shall there be any strength to withstand.
James 4:7
Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
corruption_summary: Galatians 2:11 is the Reformation’s standing answer to papal infallibility, and it is also the standing rebuke of a modern evangelical culture in which correcting a prominent leader is treated as disloyalty.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul withstood Peter to the face and recorded it in an inspired letter for the whole church to read. The Roman claim that Peter held a supreme and infallible teaching office cannot survive the verse: the man was blameworthy, he was rebuked publicly by a colleague, and the rebuke stands in the canon. The Reformers pressed exactly this, and it remains the plainest single text on the point. But the principle is not merely polemical against Rome. It bears on every arrangement in which a leader has become too significant to correct — where staff, elders, and members all know a thing is wrong and no one will say it to the face. Paul’s reason was not personality but doctrine: they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel.

Ephesians 6:13 corrects the opposite temptation, which is the appetite for confrontation for its own sake. The command in the armour passage is to stand, and the enemy named is not a man at all — we wrestle not against flesh and blood. A Christian eager to withstand everyone he disagrees with has usually misidentified the battle. Paul withstood Peter once, over the gospel, and wrote elsewhere that the servant of the Lord must not strive but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient. Both belong to the same apostle and the same week’s work. Knowing which occasion is which is most of pastoral wisdom, and the test is whether the truth of the gospel is at stake.
roots_summary: Greek anthistemi (G436), to set oneself against, to withstand; Hebrew chazaq (H2388) and amad (H5975), to be strong and to stand, in the Old Testament uses.
roots_lines: Greek anthistemi (G436) — to stand against, to withstand, to resist; Ephesians 6:13, Galatians 2:11, James 4:7.
Greek histemi (G2476) — to stand; the root, and the repeated command of Ephesians 6:11-14.
Greek panoplia (G3833) — the whole armour of a heavy infantryman; Ephesians 6:11, 13.
Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to be strong, to prevail; the verb behind withstand at 2 Chronicles 13:8.
Hebrew amad (H5975) — to stand, to endure; neither shall there be any strength to withstand (Daniel 11:15).
usage: Able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand (Ephesians 6:13) — the posture is holding ground.
I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11) — an apostle corrected publicly.
Ye think to withstand the kingdom of the LORD (2 Chronicles 13:8) — numbers and calves against a covenant.

etymology: From Latin proficere, to advance or make progress. Webster 1828: yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; useful; advantageous. Paul uses it of Scripture, of godliness, and of a runaway slave who had become useful — a pun on Onesimus’ own name.
biblical_def: Profitable is the adjective Paul attaches to the two things that actually repay a man’s investment. The first is Scripture: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The four uses are a complete pastoral toolkit — what to believe, what is wrong, how to be set right, and how to be trained in a right course — and the stated end is a man thoroughly equipped. The second is godliness: bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come (1 Timothy 4:8). Paul is not disparaging the body; he is comparing returns, and the return on godliness runs into the next world. The third use is personal and gently humorous. Onesimus, whose name means useful, ran away from Philemon and was converted under Paul’s ministry in prison, and Paul writes: Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me (Philemon 1:11). The gospel does not merely forgive a useless man; it makes him what his name always said.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PROFITABLE as yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; and also useful, advantageous, or improving. The commercial and the moral senses both stand in the entry, as they do in Paul’s usage.
webster_full: PROFITABLE, a. — Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; as a profitable trade.
Useful; advantageous; improving; as a profitable study or discourse.
PROFIT, n. — Gain; advantage; any accession of good from labor or exertion.
The Latin proficere means to go forward, to advance — profit is progress before it is money.
Onesimus, the name of the slave in Philemon, is Greek for useful or profitable, and Paul plays on it in verse 11.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
2 Timothy 3:17
That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works.
1 Timothy 4:8
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
Philemon 1:11
Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me:
Acts 20:31
Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears.
corruption_summary: 2 Timothy 3:16 is the church’s charter for the sufficiency of Scripture, and it is emptied from two sides — by a criticism that grants inspiration in some diminished sense, and by a piety that reads the Bible for comfort and never for reproof or correction.
corruption_paragraphs: All scripture is given by inspiration of God — God-breathed, in one Greek word — and Paul makes no exceptions and grades no portions. Theories that locate inspiration in the reader’s encounter, or in the text’s religious value, or in some kernel within a husk, all founder on the adjective all and on the fact that the Scripture Paul had in view was chiefly the Old Testament, including the genealogies, the ceremonial law, and the histories which modern criticism treats as least profitable. The 1689 Confession begins here, with the Holy Scripture as the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience. Everything else in the confession depends on that first chapter.

The devotional corruption is milder and more widespread. Paul lists four profits and Christians reliably want one: doctrine yes, instruction in righteousness perhaps, but reproof and correction are the two that hurt, and a great deal of modern Bible reading is arranged to avoid them. A verse-a-day of encouragement is not what the apostle described. He describes a book that tells a man he is wrong and then sets him right, and the promised outcome is not a warmed heart but a man throughly furnished unto all good works. The furnishing requires the reproof. And 1 Timothy 4:8 supplies the reason anyone would submit to it: the return on godliness covers this life and the next, which no other investment does.
roots_summary: Greek ophelimos (G5624), useful, profitable; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed, in the same verse; Onesimos (G3682), profitable, the slave’s name.
roots_lines: Greek ophelimos (G5624) — profitable, useful; 2 Timothy 3:16, 1 Timothy 4:8, Titus 3:8.
Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed, inspired of God; a hapax legomenon at 2 Timothy 3:16.
Greek artios (G739) — fitted, complete; that the man of God may be perfect (2 Timothy 3:17).
Greek exartizo (G1822) — to fit out completely, to equip; throughly furnished unto all good works.
Greek Onesimos (G3682) — Onesimus; profitable, useful — the name Paul puns on in Philemon 11.
usage: All scripture… is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction (2 Timothy 3:16) — four profits, and two of them sting.
Godliness is profitable unto all things (1 Timothy 4:8) — a return that runs into the next world.
In time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable (Philemon 1:11) — a man made what his name said.

etymology: From Latin instruere, to build into, to furnish, to equip — the same root as structure. Webster 1828: taught; educated; directed; informed. The Latin figure is architectural: to instruct a man is to build something into him.
biblical_def: Instructed in the Authorized Version is never mere information transfer; it is equipping. Our Lord uses it of the scribe who has been trained for the kingdom: every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old (Matthew 13:52) — a man with a stocked storehouse, holding both testaments and able to produce what the moment needs. Luke describes Apollos as one instructed in the way of the Lord who nevertheless knew only the baptism of John, and Aquila and Priscilla took him and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly (Acts 18:25-26) — instruction can be genuine and still incomplete, and a mighty man in the scriptures received correction from a tentmaker and his wife. Paul’s own use is the most striking, because the schooling was in circumstances rather than in doctrine: I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need (Philippians 4:12). The verb there is the word for initiation into a mystery. Contentment is not a temperament; it is a thing learned, and hunger is one of the classrooms.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines INSTRUCT as to teach; to inform the mind; to educate; to direct or enjoin; and derives it from the Latin for building or furnishing. The architectural metaphor — building something into a man — is exactly right for Matthew 13:52.
webster_full: INSTRUCT, v.t. — To teach; to inform the mind; to educate; to impart knowledge to one who was destitute of it.
To direct; to enjoin; to persuade; to give orders to; as, the minister was instructed to negotiate.
INSTRUCTED, pp. — Taught; informed; educated; directed.
From the Latin instruo, to build in, to furnish, to equip — the root of structure.
Webster’s note on the etymology recovers what English has lost: instruction furnishes a man as a storehouse is furnished.
scriptures: Matthew 13:52
Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.
Acts 18:25
This man was instructed in the way of the Lord; and being fervent in the spirit, he spake and taught diligently the things of the Lord, knowing only the baptism of John.
Philippians 4:12
I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound: every where and in all things I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer need.
Jeremiah 6:8
Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee; lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited.
2 Timothy 3:16
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
corruption_summary: Discipleship has been widely reduced to information delivery on one side and to unstructured relationship on the other, and Matthew 13:52 describes something neither of them is: a furnished householder who can bring out the right thing at the right time.
corruption_paragraphs: The scribe instructed unto the kingdom brings forth things new and old, which means he has both testaments in his treasure and knows which the hour requires. That is a competence, and it is built into a man over years by teaching, reading, memory, and use. Two modern failures stand on either side of it. One fills the storehouse and never opens it — the man who has attended everything and can apply nothing. The other opens a bare storehouse — the ministry of warm relationship without content, which has nothing to bring out when a real trouble arrives. Paul’s charge to Timothy joins the two: the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.

Philippians 4:12 corrects the assumption that instruction happens only in a room. Paul uses the vocabulary of initiation — he has been let into a secret — and the curriculum he names is being full and being hungry, abounding and suffering need. Contentment was learned, and the teacher was providence. This is why the catechism, the sermon, and the shipwreck are not rival schools. A believer who has been taught sound doctrine and never had it tested has been half instructed; a believer who has suffered much and been taught little has been half instructed the other way. Jeremiah’s plea puts the alternative starkly: Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee.
roots_summary: Greek matheteuo (G3100), to be made a disciple, at Matthew 13:52; katecheo (G2727), to instruct orally, whence catechism, at Acts 18:25; mueo (G3453), to initiate, at Philippians 4:12.
roots_lines: Greek matheteuo (G3100) — to be discipled, to be instructed as a learner; Matthew 13:52 and 28:19.
Greek katecheo (G2727) — to sound down into the ears, to instruct orally; Acts 18:25, Luke 1:4, Galatians 6:6 — the root of catechism.
Greek mueo (G3453) — to initiate into the mysteries; I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry (Philippians 4:12).
Greek paideia (G3809) — instruction, training, chastening; instruction in righteousness (2 Timothy 3:16).
Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to chasten, to instruct; be thou instructed, O Jerusalem (Jeremiah 6:8), where teaching and discipline are one word.
usage: Every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 13:52) — a furnished storehouse, new and old.
Instructed in the way of the Lord… knowing only the baptism of John (Acts 18:25) — real teaching, still incomplete.
I am instructed both to be full and to be hungry (Philippians 4:12) — contentment as a learned skill.

etymology: From Latin inhabitare, to dwell in. Webster 1828: occupied by inhabitants; dwelt in. Isaiah uses it for God’s stated purpose in creating the earth, and for the desolation He pronounces on Babylon — a land never inhabited.
biblical_def: Inhabited carries a doctrine of creation and a doctrine of judgment. Isaiah states the purpose: thus saith the LORD that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the LORD; and there is none else (Isaiah 45:18). The earth was not made as an experiment or a stage prop; it was made to be lived on, and the same chapter insists there is no other God to whom the credit or the blame could be assigned. Against that stands the sentence on Babylon: It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there (Isaiah 13:20). The judgment is precisely the reversal of the purpose — ground made for habitation and emptied. Jeremiah pronounces the same over Jerusalem if she will not hear: Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem… lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited (Jeremiah 6:8). And the word runs on to the end of the Bible, where the city that comes down from God out of heaven is inhabited for ever, and the tabernacle of God is with men, and He will dwell with them.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines INHABIT as to live or dwell in; to occupy as a place of settled residence — and INHABITED as occupied by inhabitants, human or otherwise. The permanence in settled residence is the point of Isaiah 45:18.
webster_full: INHABIT, v.t. — To live or dwell in; to occupy as a place of settled residence.
INHABITED, pp. — Occupied by inhabitants, human or animal.
INHABITANT, n. — A dweller; one who dwells or resides permanently in a place, as distinguished from a temporary lodger.
From Latin in and habitare, to dwell, a frequentative of habere, to have or hold.
Webster’s distinction between a permanent dweller and a temporary lodger is the difference the New Testament presses on Christians, who are strangers and pilgrims here.
scriptures: Isaiah 45:18

For thus saith the LORD that created the heavens; God himself that formed the earth and made it; he hath established it, he created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited: I am the LORD; and there is none else.
Isaiah 13:20
It shall never be inhabited, neither shall it be dwelt in from generation to generation: neither shall the Arabian pitch tent there; neither shall the shepherds make their fold there.
Jeremiah 6:8
Be thou instructed, O Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from thee; lest I make thee desolate, a land not inhabited.
Genesis 1:28

And God blessed them, and God said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over every living thing that moveth upon the earth.
Acts 17:26
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
corruption_summary: Isaiah 45:18 — he formed it to be inhabited — stands against the antinatalist mood of the age, which treats human habitation of the earth as the problem rather than the purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument that the world would be better with fewer people on it, and best with none, has moved from the fringe into ordinary conversation, and it is often voiced with real moral earnestness about the planet’s future. Isaiah 45:18 answers the premise rather than the arithmetic. God created it not in vain; He formed it to be inhabited; and the mandate of Genesis 1:28 is to be fruitful, multiply, and fill it. Children are consistently presented in Scripture as a heritage and a reward, and a full quiver as a blessing. None of this licenses the exploitation the earlier corruption of dominion produced; the same God who commanded the filling commanded the sabbaths of the land. But a Christian may not adopt a framework in which the birth of a human being is on the debit side of a ledger.

The judgment texts must be held with the same seriousness. Isaiah 13 pronounces on Babylon exactly the reversal of Isaiah 45 — ground made for habitation and left to the wild beasts of the desert — and Jeremiah 6:8 says God will do it to Jerusalem if she will not be instructed. Land emptied of its people is one of Scripture’s standing pictures of divine wrath, which is why the exile is described as the land keeping its sabbaths. And the last word is habitation restored: a city, not a garden merely, inhabited for ever, and God Himself dwelling with men. The Christian hope is not escape from an inhabited earth but a new one, and He that sat upon the throne said, Behold, I make all things new.
roots_summary: Hebrew yashab (H3427), to sit, to remain, to dwell; shakan (H7931), to settle down or tabernacle; Greek katoikeo (G2730), to dwell, to inhabit.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashab (H3427) — to sit, dwell, remain, inhabit; Isaiah 45:18 and 13:20.
Hebrew shakan (H7931) — to settle, to tabernacle; the root of shekinah, God’s dwelling with His people.
Hebrew tohu (H8414) — without form, waste, in vain; he created it not in vain (Isaiah 45:18), the same word as Genesis 1:2.
Greek katoikeo (G2730) — to dwell, to inhabit permanently; used of the fulness of the Godhead dwelling bodily in Christ (Colossians 2:9).
Greek katoikia (G2733) — a habitation; the bounds of their habitation (Acts 17:26).
usage: He created it not in vain, he formed it to be inhabited (Isaiah 45:18) — the stated purpose of the earth.
It shall never be inhabited (Isaiah 13:20) — judgment as the reversal of that purpose.
A land not inhabited (Jeremiah 6:8) — the same threat held over Jerusalem.

etymology: From Latin plenus, full, through Old French plente. Webster 1828: fulness; abundance; a full or adequate supply. In Scripture plenty is always a gift and always a test, and the seven years of it in Egypt were given precisely so that the seven years of famine could be survived.
biblical_def: Plenty in Scripture is God’s gift and never a man’s achievement, and it is regularly paired with what follows it. Pharaoh’s dream is the pattern: there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt: And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt (Genesis 41:29-30). Joseph’s counsel is the wisdom that follows — store a fifth in the good years, because the plenty is not for spending only but for keeping others alive. Proverbs ties plenty to two ordinary means. To the man who honours the LORD with his firstfruits: so shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine (Proverbs 3:10). To the man who works: He that tilleth his land shall have plenty of bread: but he that followeth after vain persons shall have poverty enough (Proverbs 28:19). Neither is a formula; both are the ordinary way God orders a world. And Joel gives the promise in which plenty finds its proper end: ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God (Joel 2:26). Fulness, satisfaction, and praise, in that order — and the order matters, because plenty that stops short of praise has failed.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PLENTY as abundance; copiousness; full supply; and notes its use as an adjective in familiar language, which he marks as improper. The Latin plenus, full, is the root, giving also plenary and replenish.
webster_full: PLENTY, n. — Abundance; copiousness; full or adequate supply; sufficiency.
Fruitfulness; a full harvest; as a year of plenty.
Webster notes the colloquial adjectival use — plenty good — and marks it improper in writing.
From Latin plenus, full, whence also plenary, plenitude, and replenish — the word of Genesis 1:28.
The Authorized Version also uses plenteous and plenteousness, as at Genesis 41:53 and Psalm 103:8.
scriptures: Genesis 41:29
Behold, there come seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt:
Genesis 41:30
And there shall arise after them seven years of famine; and all the plenty shall be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine shall consume the land;
Proverbs 3:10
So shall thy barns be filled with plenty, and thy presses shall burst out with new wine.
Proverbs 28:19
He that tilleth his land shall have plenty of bread: but he that followeth after vain persons shall have poverty enough.
Joel 2:26
And ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD your God, that hath dealt wondrously with you: and my people shall never be ashamed.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 3:10 is the prosperity movement’s favourite kind of verse — a promise of full barns attached to giving — and the corruption is not in the promise but in the conversion of a proverb into a contract.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs states the ordinary way God governs a world: honour the LORD with thy substance and with the firstfruits of all thine increase, and the barns are filled. That is true, and a Christian who has never tested it has missed something real. What Proverbs does not do is guarantee the outcome in every case, and the canon itself supplies the controls — Job, whose barns emptied while he was upright; the Preacher, who saw the righteous perishing in his righteousness; and the apostle who knew both how to abound and how to suffer need. A proverb is a wise generalization about how God usually orders things, not a promissory note. The prosperity teacher converts the genre and then blames the sufferer’s faith when the note is not honoured.

The deeper danger of plenty is stated by Moses before Israel ever entered the land: when thou hast eaten and art full, and hast built goodly houses and dwelt therein, beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God… and thou say in thine heart, My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth. Genesis 41:30 says the same in a sentence — all the plenty shall be forgotten — and it means the memory of the good years will not sustain anyone through the famine. Plenty is harder to survive spiritually than want, which is why Agur prayed for neither poverty nor riches, and why Joel ends the promise of plenty at praise. A full barn is safest in the hands of a grateful man.
roots_summary: Hebrew saba (H7647), plenty, abundance, and sob; Greek perisseia for abundance; the English is from Latin plenus, full.
roots_lines: Hebrew saba (H7647) — plenty, abundance, satiety; Genesis 41:29-30, Proverbs 3:10.
Hebrew saba (H7646) — the verb, to be satisfied, filled; ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied (Joel 2:26).
Hebrew rab (H7227) — much, many, abundant; the general term for plenty in the Psalms.
Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread, food; plenty of bread (Proverbs 28:19).
Latin plenus, full — the root of the English word, and of replenish in Genesis 1:28.
usage: Seven years of great plenty throughout all the land of Egypt (Genesis 41:29) — abundance given for the famine ahead.
All the plenty shall be forgotten (Genesis 41:30) — why the good years must be stored and not merely enjoyed.
Ye shall eat in plenty, and be satisfied, and praise the name of the LORD (Joel 2:26) — plenty ending where it should.
